bib.title: Think Bayes, Chapter 15: Dealing with Dimensions

question: How can Bayesian inference estimate the number of species, their prevalences, and future discoveries (the Unseen Species problem) from a sample of reads?
contributions: A hierarchical Dirichlet-multinomial model with a prior over the number of species n, and a sequence of optimisations (Species2, Species4, Species5) that make it scale to 100+ observed species.
Predictive simulation of rarefaction curves, new-species counts and coverage.

results.claim: With a Dirichlet(1,1,1) prior and counts 3 lions, 2 tigers, 1 bear, the posterior mean prevalences are 44%, 33% and 22%.
results.setup: Three known species, Dirichlet prior with all params 1 (prior marginal Beta(1,2), mean 1/3), data [3,2,1].
results.quote: The posterior mean prevalences are 44%, 33%, and 22%.

results.claim: For subject B1242 (400 reads, 61 observed species) the most likely number of species is 72, with a 90% credible interval of 66 to 79.
results.setup: Species5 hierarchical model, uniform prior on n over a range (3 to 30 used in the toy example; range for belly button data not stated), Dirichlet prevalences, Belly Button Biodiversity 2.0 pilot data.
results.quote: The most likely value is 72, with 90% credible interval 66 to 79.
results.note: Iteration count and prior range for this run are not stated.

results.claim: Probability of exactly 61 species (no unseen) is nearly zero; 87 or more species is unlikely.
results.quote: The probability that there are exactly 61 species, and no unseen species, is nearly zero.

results.claim: The most prevalent species is 23% of the 400 reads but its estimated prevalence is about 20% (90% CI 17% to 23%) because of unseen species.
results.setup: Subject B1242, mixture over n of Beta marginals.
results.quote: The most prevalent species accounts for 23% of the 400 reads, but since there are almost certainly unseen species, the most likely estimate for its prevalence is 20%, with 90% credible interval between 17% and 23%.

results.claim: After 100 additional reads the median predicted number of new species is 2 (90% CI 0 to 5); after 800 reads 3 to 12 new species are expected.
results.metric: new species vs additional reads k
results.value: median 2 at k=100; 3 to 12 at k=800
results.n: 100 simulated curves shown in Fig 15.5; simulation count for Fig 15.6 not stated
results.setup: Subject B1242, simulate n from posterior, prevalences from Dirichlet, then future reads.
results.quote: After 100 reads, the median predicted number of new species is 2; the 90% credible interval is 0 to 5.
results.note: The 800-read statement is 'we expect to see 3 to 12 new species', interval level not stated.

results.claim: By inspection of simulated rarefaction curves, 400 more reads likely find 2 to 6 new species.
results.quote: By inspection we can estimate that after 400 more reads we are likely to find 2–6 new species.

results.claim: With 200 additional reads there is about a 40% chance of reaching 90% coverage; with 1000 reads about 90%.
results.setup: Subject B1242, coverage = observed species / n, read off complementary CDFs.
results.quote: For example, with 200 reads, you have about a 40% chance of getting 90% coverage. With 1000 reads, you have a 90% chance of getting 90% coverage.

results.claim: In the toy three-species case with a uniform prior on n in 3..29, the posterior mode of n is 4, values 3 to 7 are reasonably likely, and 29 is negligible.
results.setup: ns = range(3, 30), uniform prior, Species class, 1000 Dirichlet samples per hypothesis.

results.claim: Updating one species at a time makes the random-prevalence likelihood far more efficient, with cost proportional to k*m (k hypotheses, m observed species) in Species5, versus k*m^2 for the Dirichlet-object version.
results.quote: So if we do m updates, the total run time is proportional to km2.
results.note: The superscript prints as 'km2' in the text extraction.

results.claim: Subject B1242 sample: 400 reads yielded 61 species, with many singletons (24-plus counts of 1), suggesting unseen species.

limits: Assumes every animal or bacterium is equally likely to be observed; the author concedes swabbing and amplification may bias which species are read.
'Species' is used loosely (really operational taxonomic units, OTUs).
The prior on n is uniform; the author says background information would justify a different prior.
Upper bound on n is a judgment call, checked only by looking at posterior tail mass.
The author says he skipped further details needed to validate on real data, pointing to a blog post.
Optimised versions were validated only by comparing against simpler versions, not against ground truth.
Monte Carlo likelihood uses a fixed number of iterations (1000 in the code shown); no convergence diagnostics or timings are reported.
Code is Python 2 era (print statements, dict.iteritems, numpy.int), and relies on the thinkbayes module.
practices: Use a Dirichlet prior, not independent betas, for prevalences that must sum to 1 (Sec 15.2).
Start with a simple, slow version and use it for regression testing of the optimised one (Sec 15.6).
Use the same random draws across hypotheses so comparisons are fairer and converge in fewer iterations (Sec 15.5).
Split data into sequential updates when the joint likelihood is too sharp for Monte Carlo sampling to hit, since sequential and batch updates give the same posterior (Sec 15.7).
Work in log-likelihoods and subtract the maximum before exponentiating to avoid underflow (Sec 15.6).
Drop multiplicative factors that depend only on data, such as the multinomial coefficient (Sec 15.3).
Answer predictive questions by simulating from the posterior: draw n, draw prevalences, generate reads, accumulate the joint of (k, num_new) (Sec 15.10).
Iterate on models, starting simple and adding complexity, using each model to validate the others (Sec 15.13).

code.snippet:
def SampleLikelihood(self, i, count):
    gammas = numpy.random.gamma(self.params)
    sums = numpy.cumsum(gammas)[self.ns[0]-1:]
    ps = gammas[i-1] / sums
    log_likes = numpy.log(ps) * count
    log_likes -= numpy.max(log_likes)
    likes = numpy.exp(log_likes)
    return likes
